title: On Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating wisdom, compassion, and awareness in daily life through the practice of mindfulness and self-reflection. Kanho Chris Burkhart encourages listeners to approach spiritual practices with an open and non-judgmental mind, recognizing that true growth and transformation come from embracing imperfection and uncertainty. By doing so, we can develop greater kindness, wisdom, and awareness, leading to a more authentic and compassionate way of living.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning and welcome to the [unclear: "Red Cedars and Community"] Sunday program.
It's a real pleasure to see you.
I know there are many things to do, and I really appreciate that you decided to come join us.
I titled today's Dharma talk "On Precepts."
You may know by now that I really enjoy starting my talks with a poem.
Today, however, I have a different offering: a slightly modified version of the precepts as used by the Everyday Zen community, and an excerpt from Norman Fischer's book, *Taking Our Places*.
So here it goes.
*The threefold refuge.
I take refuge in Buddha.
This is the stillness, the clarity, the kindness that is the real nature of all life.
I take refuge in Dharma.
This is the way of life day by day that accords with Buddha.
I take refuge in Sangha.
This is the community of all being.
That is our refuge and support.*
*The three boundless precepts.
I vow to refrain from all action that increases suffering.
This is the intention to always practice a wise restraint.
I vow to perform all action that increases awareness.
This is the intention to actually do what occurs to us that can make ourselves and others truly happy.
I vow to live for and with all being.
This is the intention to always try to see everything with an unselfish eye.*
*The ten clear mind precepts.
A follower of the way cultivates and encourages life, does not take life.
One who is committed to following the way lives with awareness.
Such a person can never knowingly harm a single thing.
A follower of the way honors the gift not yet given, does not steal.
Everything belongs to us and nothing belongs to us.
But we don't take anything unless it is offered to us as a gift.*
*A follower of the way remains faithful in relationships, does not misuse sexuality.
There is no way to remain deeply in relationship without complete honesty and openness.
A follower of the way communicates truth, does not lie.
Our speech must be true and accurate and kind.
We make and destroy worlds with our words.
A follower of the way polishes clarity, dispelling delusion, does not intoxicate self or others.
To share spirits moderately with friends may be alright.
But intoxication as a way to relax or cope, whether it be with substances or doctrines, creates confusion and unhappiness.*
*A follower of the way creates wisdom from ignorance, does not criticize others mindlessly.
We make an effort to be thoughtful and caring in our speech about others.
In this way we can love and be loved.
A follower of the way maintains modesty, praises others, not self.
Please let each other know frequently how much you love and respect each other and why.
A follower of the way shares freely, is not stingy.
Since there is nothing we can possess, especially others, we approach the world and each other with open hands.
A follower of the way dwells in equanimity, does not harbor anger or ill will.*
*When there is anger, see it as anger.
Respect it but don't keep it close.
Try as much as you can to let it go.
Try not to let a single day end with ill will between you.
There is no justification for resentment.
Remember this.
A follower of the way respects the Buddha, unfolds the Dharma, and nourishes the Sangha.
With the taking of these precepts we express our vow to live a life that is in accord with the sacred nature of all that is.*
Now I'm following up with an excerpt from the book *Taking Our Places*, written by Norman Fischer.
*In particle physics*, I know you guys love those little science sprinkles, *the search for the irreducible core of matter yields only a seemingly endless proliferation of parts.
The more closely you look at the parts, the less easily they can be found.
They seem to be indeterminate and relative to the very act of your looking.
While on a gross level we can distinguish one thing from another, on a refined level nothing is actually findable.
Similarly, the more closely you look into your own conduct and the conduct of others, the less you will find a me to be right or you to be wrong.
And the less you will find right or wrong, a good or a bad.
There is only the wide, true and deep effort to be effectively kind, beyond moral judgment or discrimination.* End quote.
So last Wednesday we celebrated the precepts together in our new home at the Unitarian Fellowship.
Doing that always makes me inexplicably happy.
Maybe it is a carryover from Jukai or priest ordination.
Maybe it is a way of rising up to meet the oneness, the non-duality of life.
If we do think in terms of one and not two, how can we think about breaking the precepts?
Maybe it is remembering wise words that were shared with me: if it is without love, it is not the precepts.
We need to recall how we are so profoundly tied together, how our lives are each completely intertwined and interdependent.
We are more intimate with each other than the words can ever convey.
We are all relatives.
We are all family.
Now that I have said, if we do think in terms of one and not two, how can we think about breaking the precepts?
I ought to add the other part.
Of course it happens that we break the precepts.
It happens all the time.
Sometimes we may stick too closely to the literal meaning of a precept.
At other times we just simply need rules to figure out how to go forward.
Rules or reminders.
Well, we usually don't need reminders not to kill somebody.
That seems to come natural to us.
But gossip or self-elevation may sneak its way into our conversation and our speech.
And of course the literal meaning is important.
Sometimes our interpretation of the compassionate aspect of a precept may be totally off.
We are just not understanding what it means to be compassionate, truly compassionate, in a certain situation.
Pity may creep in, or the idea that we are actually helping someone else.
We need to see that abiding by the compassionate aspect, the compassionate view of the precept, is essential.
Because following the literal meaning of the precept is not always our way.
Our understanding of what is required of us may miss the point.
Last, not least, the ultimate meaning, the emptiness level of understanding the precept.
This ultimate meaning of the precepts touches on a deep understanding of precepts.

A superficial understanding of the ultimate level can be very harmful to practitioners and the people they interact with, unless it grows out of a very solid grounding in the literal and the compassionate levels.
Yes, the cup is already broken.
But that does not mean that we use a baseball bat to interact with fine crystal.
I am very fortunate because last year and this year too I have been able to look at the precepts together with fellow practitioners.
In our events calendar it says that I'm one of the teachers.
However, I prefer to say that we are exploring the precepts together.
I too learn.
This exploration brings our lives and hearts and experiences to the table.
Speaking for myself, there is a vulnerable feeling, raw, an exposure about my conduct.
And yet together we make this offering to the community altogether.
A couple of decades ago, when I started to get serious about Zen practice, I frankly wondered why the precepts were such a big deal in our Soto Zen tradition.
They show up at Jukai, ordination, the full moon ceremony, weddings and funerals.
So what is the big deal, I asked myself.
But after hanging out with them for a while I realized that each precept is a koan to be worked with, to be submerged in, to experience in our daily life.
So one thing came up for me personally.
I grew up in a Catholic family.
It never quite took, but you're surrounded by it.
I had to go to communion classes, and in Germany they actually have religion classes in school.
When you get older you can pick whatever you want.
But when you're a little kid you go to the religion class that you fit into.
Catholic and Protestant were the two flavors.
So I was wondering, when I encountered the precepts, whether they were another version of the commandments.
I have nothing against commandments.
It's helpful for humans to have guidelines to work with.
I did notice one difference early on.
The precepts pretty much deal only with my own conduct and how I relate and interact with other beings and myself.
But the first Christian commandments, in contrast, address the relationship of the believer with God.
*I am the Lord your God.
You shall not have strange gods before me.
You shall not make thyself any graven thing, nor the likeness of anything that is in heaven above or in the earth beneath, nor of those things that are in the waters under the earth.
You shall not adore them or serve them.
You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day.*
So these are all commandments that basically regulate our relationship, our outward relationship, with God.

I found it really interesting that of the ten commandments, four were requiring, I don't know exactly how to put it without being weird, but it was less how we treat our fellow beings and more how to feel about a God.
In opposition to that, I found, speaking for myself, that the precepts keep revealing themselves mostly on the cushion.
In the quiet, the stillness, there is space for the hard to speak.
And in the silence, I hear the voice usually drowned out by the next thing to do and the busyness that comes with being alive, having a household, doing my taxes and so on.
Having a meditation practice brings clear seeing.
One perceives one's place in the world.
Illusions and delusions fall away.
Things I got away with gleefully in the past now reappear stripped of their arrogance and attitude.
Frankly, these insights are often not pretty.
They are helpful, which is better, I think.
They bring wisdom and change and transformation.
Instead of the feeling of getting away with something, it turns to, "I will not make this mistake again."
If the powerful impact of understanding a mistake doesn't hit home, if it doesn't burn your soul, then I'm not making proper use of my mistakes.
It serves to enrich and teach and tenderize the heart.
Once I truly feel remorse for an act, a mistake, I can start processing it.
This process may take a long time.
And of course, this process also includes restitution and apologies and conversations with the person I hurt, if possible.
Precepts are the quick impulse control guardrails that help and support my interactions and conduct.
They are not passive, rigid patterns we bump into.
They're more like poles or a lattice that help bean sprouts grow into the sky.
Of course, we humans have a sense of what it means to live an ethical life.
No doubt about it.
When we encounter a situation, our gut usually has a pretty good idea what is right and what is wrong.
But there are desire, aversion, and delusion that may counter our honorable impulse.
By having taken the precepts, I have an obligation to the precepts.
Oh, and one more point.
The way we practice with precepts is personal.
I can tell you that I broke a precept.
I cannot say, in our language, "Look at so-and-so, they broke a precept."
That just does not work.
What do we know about the other person?
We know nothing.
So, another question.
Why is ethical conduct necessary?
Because it affects our every thought, our every action, our speech.
Today, I create the karma that impacts my life tomorrow.
My teacher Norman Fischer said, "Meditation, ethical conduct, and wisdom refine, deepen, and balance each other until little by little the vessel of our life stands strong.
In Zen, the practice of ethical conduct is both beginning and advanced practice.

While new students are encouraged to conduct themselves straightforwardly in order to learn the practice, experienced students know that their conduct is the expression of their practice in the world, the most difficult accomplishment of all."
He also said, "Zen practice has two parts: sitting down and getting up.
When we sit down, we calm, clear, and illuminate the mind.
When we get up, we live our life in this world as an extension and expression of the beauty of our sitting.
Sitting down and getting up together comprise a full and mature human being, one who is receptive and open, but also responsible and committed."
Seen from this perspective, how do we sit down with the precepts?
Open and humble, aware of our human impulses.
And we get up with humility.
The precepts I cherish are an expression of love.
Aligning ourselves with the teaching, we commit to a new life, moment by moment.
To us Zen practitioners, practicing with the precepts offers a creative path toward maturity and freedom.
Dogen said, "Buddhas and ancestors realized the entire sky and the great earth.
Manifesting the great body in the sky, there is no inside or outside.
Manifesting the Dharma body on earth, here is not an inch of ground."
So, since I did not open with a poem, I will close with one.
It's a poem by Jane Mead, and the title of the poem is "Concerning That Prayer I Cannot Make."
*Jesus, I am cruelly lonely, and I do not know what I have done, nor do I suspect that you will answer me.

And what is more, I have spent this bare month bargaining with my soul, as if I could make her promise to love me, and now it seems that what I meant when I said soul was that the river reflects the railway bridge just as the sky says it should.
It speaks that language.
I do not know who you are.*
*I come here every day to be beneath this bridge, to sit beside this river, so I must have seen the way.
How clouds just slide under the rusty arch, without snagging on the bolts, how they are borne along on the dark water.
I must have noticed their fluent speed, and also how that tattered blue t-shirt remains snagged on the ground of the mostly sunk dead tree, despite the current's constant pulling.

Yes, somewhere in my mind there must be the image of a sky blue t-shirt caught in the wide islands of ice flying by and the light clouds flying slowly under the bridge, though today the river is fully melted.*
*I must have seen.
But I did not see.
I am not equal to my longing.
Somewhere there should be a place, the exact shape of my emptiness.
There should be a place responsible for taking one back.
The river, of course, has no mercy.
It just lifts the dead fish toward the sea.
Of course.
Of course.*
*What I meant when I said soul was there should be a place.
On the far bank, the warehouse lights blink red, then green, and all the yellow machines with their rusted scoops and lifts it under a thin layer of sunny frost.
And look.
My own palm.
There, slowly rocking.
It is my pale palm.
Palm where a black pebble is turning and turning.*
*Listen.
All you [unclear: "bear"] trees.
Burrs.
Brambles.
Pile of twigs.
Red and green lights flashing.
Muddy bottle shards.
Shoe half buried.
Listen.
Listen.
I am holy.*
*An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect Dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
